text: Last spring our neighbourhood started a shared garden on the empty lot behind the library. Nobody really knew what they were doing at first. We argued for a whole evening about whether to build raised beds or dig straight into the ground, and in the end we did half of each because nobody would back down. The raised beds won, obviously. The soil in the lot was mostly gravel and old brick, and the carrots we planted there came up stunted and forked, like little orange hands. Mrs. Okafor, who is eighty-one and has gardened her whole life, laughed at them for a week. She brought cuttings from her own tomatoes and showed the kids how to pinch out the side shoots. By July we had more courgettes than anyone could eat, and people started leaving them on doorsteps at night like a prank. The library let us put a table out front with a sign saying take what you need. Some weeks it emptied in an hour. I think the garden mattered less for the food than for the excuse it gave people to talk. I learned the names of a dozen neighbours I had walked past for years. When the first frost came in October we pulled up the last of the beans together and somebody brought soup. We are already planning next year, and this time we are starting with compost.

text: Last spring our neighbourhood started a shared garden on the empty lot behind the library. Nobody really knew what they were doing at first. We argued for a whole evening about whether to build raised beds or dig straight into the ground, and in the end we did half of each because nobody would back down. The raised beds won, obviously. The soil in the lot was mostly gravel and old brick, and the carrots we planted there came up stunted and forked, like little orange hands. Mrs. Okafor, who is eighty-one and has gardened her whole life, laughed at them for a week. She brought cuttings from her own tomatoes and showed the kids how to pinch out the side shoots. By July we had more courgettes than anyone could eat, and people started leaving them on doorsteps at night like a prank. The library let us put a table out front with a sign saying take what you need. Some weeks it emptied in an hour. I think the garden mattered less for the food than for the excuse it gave people to talk. I learned the names of a dozen neighbours I had walked past for years. When the first frost came in October we pulled up the last of the beans together and somebody brought soup. We are already planning next year, and this time we are starting with compost.

We argued for a whole evening about whether to build raised beds or dig straight into the ground, and in the end we did half of each because nobody would back down. The raised beds won, obviously. The soil in the lot was mostly gravel and old brick, and the carrots we planted there came up stunted and forked, like little orange hands. Mrs. Okafor, who is eighty-one and has gardened her whole life, laughed at them for a week. She brought cuttings from her own tomatoes and showed the kids how to pinch out the side shoots. By July we had more courgettes than anyone could eat, and people started leaving them on doorsteps at night like a prank. The library let us put a table out front with a sign saying take what you need. Some weeks it emptied in an hour. I think the garden mattered less for the food than for the excuse it gave people to talk. I learned the names of a dozen neighbours I had walked past for years. When the first frost came in October we pulled up the last of the beans together and somebody brought soup. We are already planning next year, and this time we are starting with compost.

text: Last spring our neighbourhood started a shared garden on the empty lot behind the library. Nobody really knew what they were doing at first. We argued for a whole evening about whether to build raised beds or dig straight into the ground, and in the end we did half of each because nobody would back down. The raised beds won, obviously. The soil in the lot was mostly gravel and old brick, and the carrots we planted there came up stunted and forked, like little orange hands. Mrs. Okafor, who is eighty-one and has gardened her whole life, laughed at them for a week. She brought cuttings from her own tomatoes and showed the kids how to pinch out the side shoots. By July we had more courgettes than anyone could eat, and people started leaving them on doorsteps at night like a prank. The library let us put a table out front with a sign saying take what you need. Some weeks it emptied in an hour. I think the garden mattered less for the food than for the excuse it gave people to talk. I learned the names of a dozen neighbours I had walked past for years. When the first frost came in October we pulled up the last of the beans together and somebody brought soup. We are already planning next year, and this time we are starting with compost.

text: Last spring our neighbourhood started a shared garden on the empty lot behind the library. Nobody really knew what they were doing at first. We argued for a whole evening about whether to build raised beds or dig straight into the ground, and in the end we did half of each because nobody would back down. The raised beds won, obviously. The soil in the lot was mostly gravel and old brick, and the carrots we planted there came up stunted and forked, like little orange hands. Mrs. Okafor, who is eighty-one and has gardened her whole life, laughed at them for a week. She brought cuttings from her own tomatoes and showed the kids how to pinch out the side shoots. By July we had more courgettes than anyone could eat, and people started leaving them on doorsteps at night like a prank. The library let us put a table out front with a sign saying take what you need. Some weeks it emptied in an hour. I think the garden mattered less for the food than for the excuse it gave people to talk. I learned the names of a dozen neighbours I had walked past for years. When the first frost came in October we pulled up the last of the beans together and somebody brought soup. We are already planning next year, and this time we are starting with compost.

We argued for a whole evening about whether to build raised beds or dig straight into the ground, and in the end we did half of each because nobody would back down. The raised beds won, obviously. The soil in the lot was mostly gravel and old brick, and the carrots we planted there came up stunted and forked, like little orange hands. Mrs. Okafor, who is eighty-one and has gardened her whole life, laughed at them for a week. She brought cuttings from her own tomatoes and showed the kids how to pinch out the side shoots. By July we had more courgettes than anyone could eat, and people started leaving them on doorsteps at night like a prank. The library let us put a table out front with a sign saying take what you need. Some weeks it emptied in an hour. I think the garden mattered less for the food than for the excuse it gave people to talk. I learned the names of a dozen neighbours I had walked past for years. When the first frost came in October we pulled up the last of the beans together and somebody brought soup. We are already planning next year, and this time we are starting with compost.

text: Last spring our neighbourhood started a shared garden on the empty lot behind the library. Nobody really knew what they were doing at first. We argued for a whole evening about whether to build raised beds or dig straight into the ground, and in the end we did half of each because nobody would back down. The raised beds won, obviously. The soil in the lot was mostly gravel and old brick, and the carrots we planted there came up stunted and forked, like little orange hands. Mrs. Okafor, who is eighty-one and has gardened her whole life, laughed at them for a week. She brought cuttings from her own tomatoes and showed the kids how to pinch out the side shoots. By July we had more courgettes than anyone could eat, and people started leaving them on doorsteps at night like a prank. The library let us put a table out front with a sign saying take what you need. Some weeks it emptied in an hour. I think the garden mattered less for the food than for the excuse it gave people to talk. I learned the names of a dozen neighbours I had walked past for years. When the first frost came in October we pulled up the last of the beans together and somebody brought soup. We are already planning next year, and this time we are starting with compost.

I think the garden mattered less for the food than for the excuse it gave people to talk. I learned the names of a dozen neighbours I had walked past for years. When the first frost came in October we pulled up the last of the beans together and somebody brought soup. We are already planning next year, and this time we are starting with compost.

text: Last spring our neighbourhood started a shared garden on the empty lot behind the library. Nobody really knew what they were doing at first. We argued for a whole evening about whether to build raised beds or dig straight into the ground, and in the end we did half of each because nobody would back down. The raised beds won, obviously. The soil in the lot was mostly gravel and old brick, and the carrots we planted there came up stunted and forked, like little orange hands. Mrs. Okafor, who is eighty-one and has gardened her whole life, laughed at them for a week. She brought cuttings from her own tomatoes and showed the kids how to pinch out the side shoots. By July we had more courgettes than anyone could eat, and people started leaving them on doorsteps at night like a prank. The library let us put a table out front with a sign saying take what you need. Some weeks it emptied in an hour. I think the garden mattered less for the food than for the excuse it gave people to talk. I learned the names of a dozen neighbours I had walked past for years. When the first frost came in October we pulled up the last of the beans together and somebody brought soup. We are already planning next year, and this time we are starting with compost.

text: Last spring our neighbourhood started a shared garden on the empty lot behind the library. Nobody really knew what they were doing at first. We argued for a whole evening about whether to build raised beds or dig straight into the ground, and in the end we did half of each because nobody would back down. The raised beds won, obviously. The soil in the lot was mostly gravel and old brick, and the carrots we planted there came up stunted and forked, like little orange hands. Mrs. Okafor, who is eighty-one and has gardened her whole life, laughed at them for a week. She brought cuttings from her own tomatoes and showed the kids how to pinch out the side shoots. By July we had more courgettes than anyone could eat, and people started leaving them on doorsteps at night like a prank. The library let us put a table out front with a sign saying take what you need. Some weeks it emptied in an hour. I think the garden mattered less for the food than for the excuse it gave people to talk. I learned the names of a dozen neighbours I had walked past for years. When the first frost came in October we pulled up the last of the beans together and somebody brought soup. We are already planning next year, and this time we are starting with compost.
